quiz.q: A 2 kg box is released from rest at the top of a 5 m high ramp and reaches the bottom at 8 m/s. How many joules did friction turn into heat? (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.e: The initial energy is m·g·h = 2·10·5 = 100 J, and the final energy is ½·2·8² = 64 J. Friction turned 100 − 64 = 36 J into heat.

quiz.q: You apply the force. Are you doing work in the physics sense?
ogeler: Lifting a book onto a shelf
Holding a weight in the air
quiz.e: For work to be done, there must be a displacement along the direction of the force. The book, the box, and the ball move in the direction of the force. The wall and the weight held in the air do not move. Even if you get tired, W = 0 in these cases.

quiz.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg object at rest over 10 m. What is the object's final speed, in m/s?
quiz.e: The net work is 20·10 = 200 J, and it equals the change in kinetic energy. Since ½·4·v² = 200, v² = 100 and v = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: A motor uses 600 J of energy in 3 s and does 450 J of useful work. What are its efficiency and useful power?
quiz.e: The efficiency is 450 / 600 = 75%. The useful power is 450 J / 3 s = 150 W. 200 W is the power supplied.
y: If you got 200 W, you divided the supplied 600 J by 3 s. The useful power is 450 J / 3 s.
Efficiency is the ratio of useful work to supplied energy, which is 450/600. Efficiency cannot exceed 100%.
25% is the part that is lost. Efficiency is the share of useful work, 450/600 = 75%.

basit-makineler.title: Simple machines
basit-makineler.summary: Learn about levers, pulleys, inclined planes, the wheel and axle, screws, gears, and efficiency.

cards.p: A simple machine makes work easier by changing the size, the direction, or the distance of a force. The lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, screw, and gear are all simple machines.

once.soru: What does the pulley at the top of a flagpole do?

secenekler.yazi: It changes the direction of the force
secenekler.neden: You pull the rope down to raise the flag.
A fixed pulley gives no gain in force.
No machine reduces the work.

cards.h: Gain in force, loss in distance
cards.p: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the load to the effort (W / F). If it is 4, you lift a 400 N load with 100 N, but you pull 4 times as much rope. So there is no gain in work.

once.soru: A machine lifts a 400 N load with 100 N. How many meters of rope do you pull while the load rises 1 m?

secenekler.neden: If you gain 4 times in force, you lose 4 times in distance, because 100·4 = 400·1.
When the force goes down, the distance goes up, and the work stays the same.
If the distance got shorter, you would gain work, and that never happens.

cards.h: The lever and the balance condition
cards.p: A lever is a bar that turns around a pivot (fulcrum). The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the effort is the effort arm, and the distance to the load is the load arm. At balance F·dF = W·dW.

cards.p: The order of the pivot, the load, and the effort sets the type of lever. On a seesaw the pivot is in the middle. On a wheelbarrow the load is in the middle, and the advantage is greater than 1. With tweezers the effort is in the middle, and the advantage is less than 1.

etk.soru: What is in the middle of this lever: the pivot, the load, or the effort?
ogeler: The screw (pivot) is between the handles and the blades.
The rivet (pivot) is between the handles and the jaws.
The wheel is the pivot, the load is in the middle, and you lift at the end.
The nut sits between the hinge and your hand.
The top of the cap is the pivot, and the edge being lifted is in the middle.
Your fingers press between the hinge and the tips.
Your hand squeezes in the middle, and the tips hold the load.
The lower hand is the pivot, and the upper hand applies the effort in the middle.

cards.p: A fixed pulley is attached to the ceiling and does not move with the load. Its advantage is 1, so F = W. Its benefit is that it changes the direction of the force. You pull the rope down to lift the load.

once.soru: With a fixed pulley, how many newtons do you pull with to balance a 200 N load?

secenekler.neden: A fixed pulley gives no gain in force, so F = W.
It is the movable pulley that halves the force.
A fixed pulley does not increase the force. It only changes its direction.

cards.p: A movable pulley rises with the load, and two rope strands carry the load. So F = W/2, and the advantage is 2. The price is that to lift the load by h you pull 2h of rope.

cards.key: If the pulley weighs w, then F = (W + w)/2. If the rope strands are not parallel, the advantage is less than 2.

once.soru: With a weightless movable pulley, how many newtons do you need to lift a 300 N load?

secenekler.neden: Two rope strands share the load, and 300 / 2 = 150 N.
That is true for a fixed pulley.
A movable pulley halves the force.

cards.p: A block and tackle combines fixed and movable pulleys. If n rope strands carry the movable block, then F = W/n. When the load rises by h, you pull n·h of rope.

cards.p: If you push a load up a sloped surface with no friction, F·L = W·h (L is the length of the ramp, h is the height). The longer the ramp, the smaller the force, but the longer the distance.

cards.key: The advantage of an inclined plane is L/h. For the same height, the work W·h does not change.

cards.p: A wheel and axle is a large handle and a small cylinder fixed to the same shaft. At balance F·R = W·r, and the advantage is R/r. A door handle, a steering wheel, and a screwdriver work this way.

cards.key: A well windlass works the same way. In one turn the effort moves 2πR and the load moves 2πr.

once.soru: Why does a thick-handled screwdriver turn a screw more easily than a thin-handled one?

secenekler.neden: For a wheel and axle the advantage is R/r. A larger handle gives the same turning effect with less force.
Weight does not make turning easier.
It is the radius of the handle, not its length, that makes it easier.

cards.p: When simple machines are connected, their advantages multiply. A movable pulley (2) combined with a wheel and axle with R = 4r (4) gives an advantage of 8. So an 800 N load is lifted with 100 N.

once.soru: A pulley with advantage 2 is connected to a wheel and axle with advantage 3. What is the total advantage?

secenekler.neden: For machines connected in a chain the advantages multiply, giving 2 · 3.
Advantages multiply, they do not add.
Advantages do not divide. Each machine reduces the force again.

once.soru: How far does a screw advance in one full turn?

secenekler.neden: In one turn the screw advances by the distance between two neighboring threads.
It takes many turns to drive a screw all the way in.
The circumference is the distance the end of the handle moves. It is not how far the screw advances.

cards.p: The rims of meshing gears move at the same speed. So the number of turns is inversely proportional to the radius, and n₁·r₁ = n₂·r₂. Meshing gears turn in opposite directions.

once.soru: A 20-tooth gear meshes with a 10-tooth gear. When the large gear makes 1 turn, how many turns does the small one make?

secenekler.neden: 1·20 = n·10: the small gear turns twice as fast.
The small gear makes more turns, not fewer.
The numbers of teeth are different, so the numbers of turns are different too.

cards.p: The pedal shares a shaft with the front gear, and the rear gear shares one with the wheel, and the chain links the two. If the front gear has 48 teeth and the rear gear has 16, the wheel makes 3 turns for each turn of the pedal.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='225' cy='125' r='52' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='225' cy='125' r='2' fill='var(--ink)' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='95' cy='125' r='30' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='5' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><circle cx='225' cy='125' r='10' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='4' stroke-dasharray='3 2'/><line x1='95' y1='94' x2='225' y2='114' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='95' y1='156' x2='225' y2='136' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='95' y1='125' x2='73' y2='165' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='61' y='163' width='24' height='6' fill='var(--ink)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1' rx='1'/><circle cx='95' cy='125' r='2.5' fill='var(--ink)' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='25' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Pedal 1 turn → wheel 3 turns</text><text x='160' y='45' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>48 / 16 = 3</text><text x='137' y='173' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>48 teeth</text><text x='225' y='153' font-size='11' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>16 teeth</text><text x='150' y='88' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>chain</text><text x='265' y='70' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)'>wheel</text></svg>
cards.key: On a hill you shift to a larger rear gear. The wheel then turns less, and pedaling gets easier. Gears linked by a chain turn in the same direction.

cards.p: In a real machine, friction turns part of the work into heat. Efficiency is the useful work divided by the work input, times 100, and it is always below 100%.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='28' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Ramp: W = 600 N, h = 1 m, L = 4 m, F = 200 N</text><text x='30' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='bold'>Work input: F·L = 200·4 = 800 J</text><rect x='30' y='72' width='195' height='34' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='225' y='72' width='65' height='34' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='127' y='94' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>useful 600 J</text><text x='257' y='94' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>heat 200 J</text><text x='30' y='128' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>Useful work: W·h = 600·1 = 600 J</text><text x='160' y='160' font-size='15' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Efficiency = 600 / 800 = 75%</text><text x='160' y='184' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Without friction F = 150 N would be enough</text></svg>
cards.key: If you apply 200 N to raise a 600 N load by 1 m on a 4 m ramp, the efficiency is 600 J / 800 J = 75%.

cards.p:
• The advantage is W / F, and there is no gain in work.
• For a lever F·dF = W·dW.
• The advantage is 1 for a fixed pulley, 2 for a movable pulley, and n for a block and tackle.
• F·L = W·h for an inclined plane, F·R = W·r for a wheel and axle, and F·2πR = W·a for a screw.
• For gears n₁·r₁ = n₂·r₂.

quiz.q: A 600 N load is lifted with a block and tackle whose movable block is carried by 4 rope strands. If the movable pulleys weigh 40 N in total, what is the smallest force, in N, you must apply to the rope? (no friction)
quiz.e: The weight of the pulleys adds to the load, so F = (W + w) / n = (600 + 40) / 4 = 160 N.

quiz.q: Put each case in the right group by lever type.
ogeler: Lifting a rock with a crowbar
quiz.e: For a crowbar and a balance the pivot is in the middle. For a paper guillotine and for rising onto your toes the load is in the middle. On your toes, the toes are the pivot and the effort is the muscle at the heel. With a broom and a shovel the upper hand is the pivot, and the lower hand applies the effort in the middle.

quiz.q: A 300 N load hangs from one end of a 2 m weightless bar. The pivot is 0.5 m from the load. What is the smallest force, in N, applied perpendicular to the other end that balances the bar?
quiz.e: The effort arm is 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 m. Since F·1.5 = 300·0.5, F = 100 N. The advantage is 1.5 / 0.5 = 3.

quiz.q: Gears K, L, and M mesh in a row and have radii r, 3r, and 2r. If K makes 6 turns clockwise, what does M do?
quiz.e: For gears in contact n·r is constant. Since 6·r = n·2r, n = 3. L turns opposite to K. M turns opposite to L, which is the same direction as K: clockwise.
y: The middle gear L reverses the direction twice. So K and M turn in the same direction, not in opposite directions.
The number of turns is inversely proportional to the radius. If 6·r = n·2r, then n = 3, and the direction is the same as K.
The number of turns is inversely proportional to the radius. So the larger gear M makes fewer turns than K.

momentum.title: Momentum and collisions
momentum.summary: Momentum, impulse, conservation, and elastic or inelastic collisions.

cards.p: Momentum is mass times velocity. It is given by p = m·v, and its unit is kg·m/s. A slow truck is harder to stop than a fast ball, because its mass is large and so its momentum is large too.

momentum</text></svg>
cards.key: Momentum is p = m·v, and its unit is kg·m/s. Being fast does not by itself mean a large momentum.

cards.p: Momentum points the same way as the velocity. Choose one direction as + and count the opposite as −. Momenta add as vectors. Two objects with equal and opposite momenta have a total momentum of zero.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-3' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c1)'/></marker><marker id='mom-4' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>right: +, left: −</text><rect x='50' y='65' width='40' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='70' y='87' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>2 kg</text><line x1='92' y1='82' x2='142' y2='82' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#mom-3)'/><text x='117' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>3 m/s</text><rect x='230' y='65' width='40' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='250' y='87' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>3 kg</text><line x1='228' y1='82' x2='178' y2='82' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#mom-4)'/><text x='203' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>2 m/s</text><text x='70' y='125' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>p₁ = +6 kg·m/s</text><text x='250' y='125' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>p₂ = −6 kg·m/s</text><text x='160' y='160' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>total: (+6) + (−6) = 0</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>both are moving, yet the total momentum is zero</text></svg>
cards.key: Choose the + direction before you start a calculation. Velocity and momentum in the opposite direction get a minus sign.

once.soru: Two 1 kg balls move toward each other at 3 m/s. What is the total momentum, in kg·m/s?

secenekler.neden: The momenta point in opposite directions. +3 and −3 add up to zero.
Opposite momenta do not add up, they cancel.
The two balls carry momenta of equal size in opposite directions.

cards.p: A net force acting for a time gives an impulse, I = F·Δt. The impulse equals the change in momentum (I = Δp). Its unit is N·s, which is the same as kg·m/s.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-5' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker><marker id='mom-6' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c3)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>0.5 kg ball, frictionless surface</text><circle cx='45' cy='85' r='14' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='45' y='125' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>before: v = 0</text><line x1='70' y1='85' x2='140' y2='85' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' marker-end='url(#mom-5)'/><text x='105' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>F = 50 N</text><text x='105' y='106' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>Δt = 0.1 s</text><circle cx='185' cy='85' r='14' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='205' y1='85' x2='275' y2='85' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#mom-6)'/><text x='240' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>10 m/s</text><text x='210' y='125' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>after: v = 10 m/s</text><line x1='20' y1='140' x2='300' y2='140' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='160' y='162' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>I = F·Δt = 50 × 0.1 = 5 N·s</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Δp = 0.5 × 10 − 0 = 5 kg·m/s</text></svg>
cards.key: Impulse is a vector too, and it points along the net force, which is the direction of Δp. If the force changes, use the average force.

once.soru: A 50 N force acts on a ball at rest for 0.1 s. What is its momentum, in kg·m/s?

secenekler.neden: I = F·Δt = 50·0.1 = 5 N·s, and the change in momentum equals this.
The force is multiplied by the time, not divided.
Force alone is not momentum. It has to be multiplied by the time.

cards.h: Area under the F–t graph = impulse
cards.p: If the force changes, the impulse is the area under the force–time graph. Area below the axis is impulse in the opposite direction, and it is subtracted. For a constant force the area is a rectangle equal to F·Δt.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-7' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><polygon points='40,160 110,70 180,70 250,160' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='40' y1='160' x2='295' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-7)'/><line x1='40' y1='160' x2='40' y2='22' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-7)'/><text x='48' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>F (N)</text><text x='300' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>t (s)</text><line x1='40' y1='70' x2='110' y2='70' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><text x='34' y='74' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>20</text><text x='110' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>2</text><text x='180' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>4</text><text x='250' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>6</text><text x='145' y='120' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>area = impulse</text><text x='145' y='140' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>20 + 40 + 20 = 80 N·s</text><text x='300' y='40' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='bold'>I = Δp = 80 N·s</text></svg>
cards.key: The area under a force–time graph gives the impulse, which is Δp. The area under a force–extension graph is work. Do not mix them up.

once.soru: On an F–t graph the force rises steadily from 0 to 10 N over 4 s. What is the impulse, in N·s?

secenekler.neden: The area is a triangle, and ½ · 4 · 10 = 20 N·s.
That would be right for a rectangle. But the force is not 10 N the whole time.
Impulse is the area, not the force. Take the time into account too.

cards.p: The Δp needed to stop is fixed. Since F = Δp / Δt, a longer time means a smaller force. That is why an airbag, helmet foam, and bending your knees protect you.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-8' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><polygon points='50,170 65,50 80,170' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='110,170 155,130 200,170' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='300' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-8)'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='40' y2='22' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-8)'/><text x='48' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>F</text><text x='300' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>t</text><text x='74' y='64' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='bold'>hard ground</text><text x='170' y='128' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='bold'>airbag</text><text x='300' y='30' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>equal areas → same Δp</text><text x='300' y='50' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>short Δt → large F</text><text x='300' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='end'>long Δt → small F</text></svg>
cards.key: An airbag does not reduce the impulse (Δp). It makes the time longer and so reduces the force.

cards.h: The momentum form of the second law
cards.p: The general form of the second law is Fnet = Δp / Δt. If the mass is constant, Δp = m·Δv, and this gives F = m·a. If the net force is zero, the momentum does not change.

cards.key: F = m·a is the form that F = Δp/Δt takes when the mass is constant.

once.soru: If the net force on an object is zero, what happens to its momentum?

secenekler.neden: Since Fnet = Δp/Δt, if the force is zero then Δp is zero too.
For it to decrease, there must be a net force opposing the motion.
The momentum of a moving object is conserved when there is no force.

cards.h: A ball bouncing off a wall
cards.p: When the direction changes, watch the sign. For a ball that hits a wall at speed v and bounces back at the same speed, Δp = m(−v) − m(v) = −2mv. If the ball stuck, Δp would be only mv.

cards.p: If the external forces add up to zero, the total momentum of a system is conserved. The forces that colliding objects exert on each other are an action–reaction pair. These equal and opposite impulses cancel.

cards.key: The momentum one object gains, the other loses. Because a collision is brief, external forces such as friction are usually neglected.

once.soru: Two skaters at rest on an ice rink push each other apart. What happens to their total momentum?

secenekler.neden: There is no external force. So the total momentum, zero at the start, stays zero.
Both of them move, but their momenta point in opposite directions.
The momentum was already zero at the start, and it is conserved.

cards.p: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Billiard balls come close to this. The swap of velocities you just saw happens only if the masses are equal.

girdiler.etiket: Mass of the object at rest

cards.p: If a system at rest breaks apart, the total momentum stays zero. The pieces fly apart with equal and opposite momenta. The recoil of a rifle and a rocket work this way.

cards.key: A rocket does not need air. In an explosion the kinetic energy increases, and this energy comes from the fuel or from a spring. Since KE = p²/2m, the lighter piece has the larger kinetic energy.

cards.h: Velocity of the center of mass
cards.p: The velocity of the center of mass is vCM = Σp / Σm. With no external force, vCM stays constant. When a firework explodes in the air, the center of mass of its pieces keeps following the old path.
cards.key: The center of mass is the average position that behaves as if all the mass were gathered at one point.

once.soru: A firework flying through the air explodes. How does the center of mass of the pieces move?

secenekler.yazi: It continues on its old path
secenekler.neden: The explosion is an internal event. It does not change the motion of the center of mass.
An explosion does not destroy momentum.
The pieces scatter, but the center of mass follows the old path.

cards.p: In a collision in a plane, momentum is conserved in each component separately. If the incoming ball moves only in the x direction, then after the collision the y momenta of the two balls are equal and opposite.

cards.key: Add the momentum components, not the speeds. Write separate equations for x and y.

once.soru: In billiards the cue ball comes in along x and hits a ball at rest. What is the total y momentum after the collision?

secenekler.neden: There was no momentum in the y direction at the start. Each component is conserved separately.

secenekler.yazi: The same as the cue ball's
secenekler.neden: The momentum in the x direction is conserved, and the total in the y direction stays zero.
Without an external force, y momentum cannot appear.

cards.p:
• Momentum p = m·v is a vector, and its unit is kg·m/s.
• Impulse is I = F·Δt = Δp, and it equals the area under the force–time graph.
• For the same Δp, a longer time means a smaller force.
• With no external force, the total momentum is conserved.
• In an elastic collision KE is conserved too. In other collisions it decreases, and in an explosion it increases.

quiz.q: On a frictionless level track, a 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at rest and sticks to it. What is their common velocity, in m/s?
quiz.e: Momentum is conserved: 3·4 + 1·0 = (3 + 1)·v. This gives v = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s.

quiz.q: What happens to the total kinetic energy of the system in each event?
quiz.e: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved. For vehicles that stick together or get crushed, part of the kinetic energy turns into heat, sound, and deformation. In an explosion or a shot, pieces at rest start to move. The energy comes from the fuel, and the kinetic energy increases.

quiz.q: The net force on a 2 kg object at rest rises steadily from 0 to 50 N in 0.2 s, then falls steadily back to zero in the next 0.2 s. What is the object's final speed, in m/s?
quiz.e: The force–time graph is a triangle, and the impulse is ½ · 0.4 · 50 = 10 N·s. This equals Δp. So v = 10 / 2 = 5 m/s.

quiz.q: A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall head-on at 6 m/s and bounces back at 4 m/s. The contact lasts 0.05 s. What is the average force, in N, that the wall exerts on the ball?
quiz.e: Taking the backward direction as −, Δp = 0.5·(−4) − 0.5·6 = −5 kg·m/s, with a magnitude of 5 N·s. The force is F = 5 / 0.05 = 100 N. Subtracting the speeds (6 − 4) is wrong, because the direction changed.

tork-denge.title: Torque, equilibrium, and center of mass
tork-denge.summary: How does a force cause rotation, and when does an object stay balanced or tip over?

cards.p: The turning effect of a force is called torque, given by τ = F·d. Here d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force, and it is called the lever arm. With a longer arm, less force is enough.

cards.key: Torque is also called the moment of a force. For the same torque, a longer lever arm needs less force (F = τ / d).

cards.p: If the force makes an angle θ with r, the lever arm is d = r·sinθ, and τ = F·r·sinθ. The component perpendicular to r does the turning. sin90° = 1 and sin0° = 0.

once.soru: A torque of 30 N·m clockwise and 20 N·m counterclockwise act on a bar. What is the net torque, in N·m?

secenekler.neden: Opposite torques are subtracted: 30 − 20 = 10 N·m, clockwise.
Opposite torques do not add up, they are subtracted.
If the torques were equal, the total would be zero. But 30 and 20 are not equal.

cards.h: Unit: N·m, but not the joule
cards.p: The unit of torque is the N·m. The joule is also N·m, but in work the force is multiplied by the distance along the same line, and in torque by the perpendicular distance. So torque is not written in joules.

once.soru: Which is the unit of torque?

secenekler.neden: Torque is force times perpendicular distance. Its unit is the newton times the meter.
The joule is for work and energy. Torque is written in N·m.
The newton is the unit of force. In torque the force is multiplied by a distance.

cards.p: To find the tension in a rope holding a hinged bar, take torques about the hinge, because the torque of the hinge force is zero. The torque of the rope is T·L·sinα, and the torque of the bar is W·L/2.

cards.key: The tension depends on the angle the rope makes with the bar. The smaller the angle, the larger T.

once.soru: The end of a 100 N horizontal bar hinged to a wall is held by a rope at 30° to the bar. What is the tension in the rope, in N?

secenekler.neden: About the hinge, T·L·sin30° = 100·L/2. This gives T = 100 N.
The weight acts at the middle, but the rope pulls at an angle. So sin30° = 0.5 comes into it.
The weight of the bar acts at its middle, not at its end.

cards.h: Center of mass and center of gravity
cards.p: The center of mass is the point where an object behaves as if all its mass were there. In uniform gravity the weight also acts at this point, which is called the center of gravity. For a ring this point is in empty space.

once.soru: Where is the center of mass of a uniform ring?

secenekler.neden: A ring is symmetric. Its center of mass is at the geometric center, even though there is no material there.
Every point of the ring is symmetric, and no point stands out.

secenekler.yazi: It has no center of mass
secenekler.neden: Every object has a center of mass.

cards.h: Center of mass of a composite object
cards.p: For an object made of parts, the center of mass is xCM = Σm·x / Σm. The center of mass is closer to the heavier part. A part that has been removed counts as a negative mass.

cards.h: Base of support and tipping over
cards.p: If the vertical line down from the center of gravity falls inside the base of support, the object does not tip over. If it falls outside, the object tips. A low center of gravity and a wide base make tipping harder.

cards.key: The tipping limit is the moment the vertical line through the center of gravity passes exactly through the edge of the base. That is why race cars are low.

cards.p: A box on an incline slides when tanα > μs and tips when tanα > b/h (b is the base, h is the height). As the angle grows, whichever limit is reached first happens.
cards.key: If μs < b/h, the box slides without tipping; if μs > b/h, it tips without sliding.

once.soru: You put a low box with a wide base on an icy ramp. If the ramp slowly gets steeper, what does the box do first?

secenekler.neden: On ice there is very little friction, so the sliding limit is reached early. For a low box to tip, the ramp would have to be very steep.
A low box has a low center of gravity. The ramp would have to get very steep for it to tip.
There is little friction on ice. The box starts to move as soon as the ramp gets a bit steeper.

cards.p: If an object returns after a small push, its equilibrium is stable. If it moves away, it is unstable. If it stays in its new place, it is neutral. In stable equilibrium the center of gravity is at its lowest.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M15,80 Q55,150 95,80' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='55' cy='105' r='10' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M120,130 Q160,70 200,130' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='160' cy='90' r='10' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='225.0' y1='115.0' x2='305.0' y2='115.0' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='265' cy='105' r='10' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='55.0' y='150.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>stable</text><text x='55.0' y='167.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>returns</text><text x='55.0' y='183.0' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>hanging pendulum</text><text x='160.0' y='150.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>unstable</text><text x='160.0' y='167.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>moves away</text><text x='160.0' y='183.0' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>inverted pendulum</text><text x='265.0' y='150.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>neutral</text><text x='265.0' y='167.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>stays in new place</text><text x='265.0' y='183.0' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>ball on flat ground</text><text x='160.0' y='26.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>push the ball a little: what happens?</text></svg>
cards.key: A ball in a hollow is in stable equilibrium, a ball on a hilltop is unstable, and a ball on flat ground is neutral. After a push, the center of gravity rises in the stable case and drops in the unstable case.

etk.soru: What happens after a small push? Choose the type of equilibrium.
ogeler: Ball at the bottom of a hollow
Ruler hung from its top end
When pushed, the center of gravity rises, and the ruler swings back.
Ball on top of a hill
When pushed, the center of gravity drops, and the pencil falls.
As it rolls, the center of gravity stays at the same height.
Wheel mounted on an axle at its center
As it turns, the center of gravity does not move.

once.soru: You give a small push to a ball at the bottom of a hollow. What happens?

secenekler.neden: When pushed, the ball rises. Its weight pulls it back to the lowest point.
A ball on a hilltop would move away. A ball in a hollow cannot climb out.

secenekler.yazi: It stays in its new place
secenekler.neden: A ball on flat ground would do that. In a hollow the ground rises toward the edges.

cards.p:
• Torque is τ = F·d = F·r·sinθ, and its unit is N·m. Its direction is clockwise or counterclockwise.
• Equilibrium needs both ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.
• The weight of a uniform bar acts at its middle.
• The center of mass is xCM = Σm·x / Σm.
• If the vertical line falls outside the base, the object tips over.

quiz.q: A 50 N force is applied to the end of a 0.4 m wrench at an angle of 30° to the wrench. What is the torque about the nut, in N·m?
quiz.e: τ = F·r·sinθ = 50·0.4·0.5 = 10 N·m. If the force were perpendicular to the wrench, the torque would be 20 N·m.

quiz.q: What happens after a small push? Choose the type of equilibrium for each object.
ogeler: Picture hung on a nail from its top
Broom balanced upright on a finger
Ruler on an axle through its center of mass
quiz.e: When a cone on its base or a hanging picture is pushed, the center of gravity rises and the object returns. These are in stable equilibrium. When a cone on its tip or an upright broom is pushed, the center of gravity drops and the object falls. These are in unstable equilibrium. When a cone on its side rolls or a ruler on an axle turns, the height of the center of gravity does not change. These are in neutral equilibrium.

quiz.q: A force is applied to a hinged bar. r is the distance from the hinge to the point where the force acts. Put the torques in order from smallest to largest.
ogeler: 20 N, r = 0.5 m, line of action through the hinge
20 N, r = 0.8 m, at 30° to the bar
20 N, r = 0.5 m, perpendicular to the bar
30 N, r = 0.6 m, perpendicular to the bar
quiz.e: Use τ = F·r·sinθ. For the force whose line passes through the hinge, τ = 0. The others are 20·0.8·0.5 = 8, 20·0.5 = 10, and 30·0.6 = 18 N·m.

quiz.q: A 6 m uniform bar weighing 120 N is supported at its ends A and B. A 300 N load is 2 m from end A. What force, in N, does support B exert on the bar?
quiz.e: Taking torques about A, N<sub>B</sub>·6 = 120·3 + 300·2 = 960, so N<sub>B</sub> = 160 N. From ΣF = 0, N<sub>A</sub> = 420 − 160 = 260 N.
